content: Hemoglobin C (HbC) is an abnormal variant of hemoglobin caused by a specific genetic mutation. This mutation involves the substitution of glutamic acid with lysine at the 6th position of the β-globin chain, referred to as the E6K substitution. In individuals who are heterozygous for this mutation, approximately 28–44% of their total hemoglobin is composed of HbC, and they do not develop anemia. However, in individuals who are homozygous for the mutation, nearly all of their hemoglobin is in the HbC form, which leads to moderate normocytic hemolytic anemia. In some cases, individuals may inherit one gene for HbC and another for hemoglobin S (HbS), resulting in a condition known as hemoglobin SC disease (HbSC). This condition is characterized by atypical hemolytic anemia and an increased tendency for red blood cells to sickle, although the sickling is less severe compared to individuals with sickle cell disease (HbSS). Additionally, individuals with HbC may also inherit a gene for thalassemia, leading to other forms of atypical hemolytic anemia. Hemoglobin C is most commonly found in populations of West African descent, particularly among the Yoruba people. It has been observed to provide some protection against severe malaria. The C in HbC refers to Christchurch, New Zealand, where this hemoglobin variant was first identified. The clinical significance of HbC lies in its impact on red blood cells. The mutation reduces the normal flexibility and plasticity of red blood cells, leading to a hemoglobinopathy. In heterozygous individuals, no anemia is present, but in homozygous individuals, mild hemolytic anemia occurs. Blood smears from homozygous individuals often reveal target cells, microspherocytes, and HbC crystals. In cases of hemoglobin SC disease, the individual inherits the HbS gene from one parent and the HbC gene from the other. Since HbC does not polymerize as easily as HbS, there is less red blood cell sickling compared to HbSS disease. Peripheral blood smears in HbSC disease typically show a predominance of target cells and only a small number of sickle cells. Patients with HbSC disease experience fewer acute vaso-occlusive crises compared to those with HbSS disease. However, they are more prone to complications such as retinopathy, ischemic bone necrosis, and priapism. The HbC gene is present in approximately 2–3% of Black individuals in the United States, while the HbS gene is found in about 8% of this population. Consequently, hemoglobin SC disease is more common than hemoglobin CC disease. The HbC gene is particularly prevalent in West African regions, including Ghana and Nigeria, where the Yoruba people historically resided.
